analysis.one_liner: Extends federal workplace safety rules and inspections to state and local government employees.
analysis.headline: Despite 48 cosponsors, the bill never left a House subcommittee and never received a vote in the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal workplace safety law (OSHA) covers private-sector workers but leaves out employees of state and local governments — teachers, firefighters, police, sanitation crews, and office workers. This bill would change the law's definition of 'employer' to include states and their cities and counties, putting millions of public employees under the same safety inspections, standards, and complaint rights private workers have. The bill was introduced in February 1999 and sent to a House subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local government employees, who today have no federal workplace safety protections and no right to a federal safety inspection. Under the bill, they would get the same OSHA standards, inspections, and complaint procedures private-sector workers have.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the definition of 'employer' in the Occupational Safety and Health Act so it includes states and their political subdivisions, extending OSHA coverage to state and local government workers.
Coverage under OSHA means public employees would be subject to federal safety standards, workplace inspections, and complaint procedures, protections they currently lack.
The bill was introduced by Rep. Robert Andrews and drew 48 cosponsors — 46 Democrats and 2 Republicans.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, which would bear the cost of meeting federal safety standards — fixing hazards, paying for inspections and any citations — costs ultimately carried by local budgets and taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Defining states and their subdivisions as 'employers' under OSHA would make them subject to federal safety standards and citations, a real cost for local governments and taxpayers, including small municipalities with tight budgets.
The bill never received a hearing or debate, so its costs and how they would be phased in were never examined publicly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is safety protections for millions of public workers who today have no federal right to an inspection; the cost is compliance spending by governments that would have to meet the standards. In a fair debate, that trade-off would be worth weighing. Instead, the bill was never debated at all — the cost estimates were never tested and the protections never happened.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House education committee and then to a subcommittee on workplace protections, and it stayed there until the two-year Congress ended without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the bill on February 23, 1999 to extend OSHA coverage to state and local government workers.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
On March 12, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where no further action was taken.
The bill attracted 48 cosponsors (46 Democrats, 2 Republicans) but received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments are better off because the bill died — they avoided the cost of federal safety compliance. State and local government workers gained nothing and remain outside federal workplace safety law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State and local governments, not their workers

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend OSHA coverage to state and local government workers.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referring the bill to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place, so the party split is untested; 46 of the 48 cosponsors were Democrats and only 2 were Republicans.

industries.note: As 'employers' under OSHA, state and local governments would have to pay to meet federal safety standards and fix hazards, and would face citations for violations. Their cost is the public workers' safety gain, so their interest in the bill runs against the workers it covers.
Federal safety coverage gives union-represented public workers enforceable standards and a federal complaint process they currently lack. Their gain is the workers' gain.
